# The Lost Country of Night

The first thing that happens in a blackout is that the century leaves the room. The refrigerator lets go of its low drone; the traffic outside thins, because every other house has gone quiet too; for a moment you can hear rain actually landing on leaves, or a dog barking blocks away, or the strange oceanic wash of your own blood moving in your ears. And then, if you have the sense to step outside, the sky. When an earthquake knocked out power across Los Angeles in January 1994, emergency dispatchers and observatories, so the story goes, fielded calls about a vast strange glow that had appeared overhead — a luminous river, people said, like smoke made of light. The callers were describing the Milky Way. They had lived beneath it their whole lives and had never once seen it.

For nearly all of human history, darkness was not an inconvenience. It was a border — a foreign country that annexed half of every life and ran its own government there. Night was the default condition of the species: the visible world shrank, each evening, to the radius of a fire, and everything beyond that radius belonged to the dark. Daylight was the exception, a loan against the coming evening. We are, as a species, night people who have recently — in the last century and a half, a rounding error in evolutionary time — gone over to the other side, and in doing so we have forgotten how deep the night used to go.

The old night had institutions. Many towns rang a curfew bell, and the word itself tells you what it meant: couvre-feu, "cover-fire" — the signal to bank your flames so the sleeping houses would not burn. Watchmen walked their rounds and called the hour and the weather into the darkness, ending on the useful fiction "all's well." Before mechanical clocks spread, the night's hours were "temporary" — twelve of them between sunset and sunrise, long in winter and short in summer — so that an hour was a measure of darkness, not of minutes. Night was not simply the day with the brightness turned down. It was a different jurisdiction, with different physics, different dangers, and different laws.

It was also a different moral territory. Thieves used it as sanctuary; lovers used it as a door. The dead were believed to walk in it, and dreams were taken seriously — visits, messages, the soul stepping briefly out of the body while it slept. Folklore made night the workplace of ghosts and witches not because our ancestors were foolish, but because the dark genuinely was a place where evidence ran out and imagination took over the watch. Fear and freedom were mixed together in it, the way they are in any wilderness.

One of the strangest discoveries about that vanished world came out of the archives. The historian Roger Ekirch spent years reading diaries, court records, medical texts, and sermons from before the industrial era, and he kept running into a phrase: "first sleep." People fell asleep not long after dark, slept hard for a few hours, then rose for a while — an interval sometimes called "the watch" — before going down again into a "second sleep" until dawn. The references run from Homer through Chaucer to Cervantes and into the notebooks of ordinary eighteenth-century households, which describe what people did in the gap: they prayed, smoked, read scripture, tended the fire, talked, made love, visited neighbors by moonlight. Anthropologists working among peoples without electricity, including the Tiv of Nigeria, found the same two-sleep vocabulary. Segmented sleep, Ekirch concluded, was not a quirk of the past. It was how humans slept.

Then came artificial light, and the two sleeps closed into one. It happened within a few generations, as lamps moved into bedrooms and evenings lengthened into hours of reading and card-playing and quiet worry. Which means the modern insomniac — the person who wakes at 3 a.m., panics, counts the hours of lost sleep, and stares at the ceiling in frustration — may be experiencing something like a phantom limb. The waking is ancient. What's new is the world around the waking: no fire to tend, no neighbor to visit, no dark and spacious hour to be awake in — only the lit hum of a house that has decided everyone must be unconscious. The Old English even had a word, uhtceare, for the sorrow of lying awake in the dark before dawn, attested in one of their poems more than a thousand years old. Your 3 a.m. has ancestors. There was once a whole room of the night set aside for it.

Ask any insomniac what the 3 a.m. mind does and they will tell you: accounting. Worries that shrink in daylight swell to cathedral size at night, and the filmmaker Ingmar Bergman gave that hour a name — the hour of the wolf — describing it as the hour when nightmares are most real, when the dying and the newborn arrive, when ghosts are at their strongest. Whatever the underlying physiology — cortisol begins its slow climb before dawn; the mind, unmediated by tasks and other people, turns inward on itself — the insomniac of the old night at least had a story to live inside. The hour was named. It had uses. Now it is only an error to be corrected, a malfunction of the machine.

To understand how thoroughly we have remade the night, you have to price light the way our ancestors did. A candle was expensive. Tallow candles smoked and stank; rushlights — dried reeds dipped in fat — gave a flame the size of a thumbnail, and reading by firelight could cost more than the book. The economist William Nordhaus traced the price of light across the centuries and found it falling more steeply than almost any commodity ever measured: by his accounting, an hour of reading after dark once cost an hour or more of human labor, where today it costs a fraction of a second. So people arranged their lives around the moon instead. The harvest moon — the full moon nearest the autumn equinox, rising close behind sunset for several evenings in a row — was once a working phenomenon: free overtime, a stretch of bright nights to bring the crop in before it spoiled. Moonlight was not romance. It was infrastructure.

And because light was wealth, we went out and hunted it. The whaling fleets of the nineteenth century were, in a literal sense, light industries: they pursued whales for the oil that burned in lamps and candles in parlors across the Western world. When petroleum gave up kerosene, it out-burned the whales; when Edison's Pearl Street Station threw its switches in 1882, whole city districts began to burn coal at a distance, and night lost another province. Each technology of light — the rushlight, the tallow candle, the whale-oil lamp, gas, the filament, the tube, the LED — redrew the border of the day a little further into the dark. What we called progress was, from the night's point of view, a series of annexations.

The war is over, and the night lost. The famous satellite photographs of Earth at night — continents veined with light, coastlines traced like circuit boards — are celebrated as the portrait of our civilization, and they are that, but read them the other way and they are a map of conquest: every bright pixel is a place where the dark used to be. A third of humanity can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live. In North America the figure is closer to four in five. Most people born in the last several decades have never seen the galaxy they live inside — its river of two hundred billion suns — except as a picture. The stars have withdrawn the way animals withdraw from logged forest: not all at once, but quietly, and by preference.

It is tempting to file all this under nostalgia, but darkness is not scenery. It is habitat, and we have been bulldozing it. Sea turtle hatchlings emerge from the sand and scramble toward the brighter horizon — which for a hundred million years meant moonlit water, and now means the glow of a beachfront town — and thousands upon thousands of them crawl inland instead and die of exhaustion, exposure, or traffic. Researchers who filmed insects around lamps discovered in 2024 that moths and dragonflies are not "attracted" to light at all, the way we have always said. Many insects steer by keeping their backs to the brightest thing in view — an ancient reflex for staying level, because the brightest thing, for four hundred million years, was the sky. A porch lamp is a false sky. The moth banks forever around a horizon that isn't there, spiraling down in what looks like lunacy and is actually a reflex as old as wings.

Migrating birds, navigating by starlight and by the soft natural glow of the horizon, are drawn into cities on foggy nights; by some estimates as many as a billion birds die in collisions with buildings in North America each year, which is why "lights out" programs in Chicago and New York exist — an attempt to give the birds back the sky. Coral reefs spawn in synchrony by the light of a particular moon, whole ecosystems timing their reproduction to a signal we have flooded with noise. Fireflies write their courtship in darkness, and under floodlights the letters are illegible. Turn a light on and you do not merely push back the dark; you destroy, within its radius, an environment that hundreds of millions of years of evolution fitted its creatures to. Light pollution is habitat loss with a lightswitch.

And the dark is not a small habitat. The overwhelming majority of the living space of this planet — the deep ocean, most of the volume in which life on Earth exists — has never seen the sun. Its inhabitants live in darkness the way we live in air. Many make their own light instead, and some biologists have suggested that bioluminescent signaling, those cold blue and green flashes of the abyss, may be the most common form of communication on Earth. When we talk about destroying the dark, we are talking about the majority world.

We remade the darkness outside, and we are only slowly discovering that we remade one inside as well. Your body is a clock that runs on planetary time — its genes turn over in roughly 24-hour cycles, an inheritance so ancient that even the cells of a fruit fly keep it. Darkness is not the absence of a stimulus to that clock; it is the signal. Melatonin flows when the light goes down; suppress the dark and you suppress the tide. The World Health Organization's cancer agency has classified night-shift work — the systematic replacement of night with light — as a probable carcinogen. We changed the night, in other words, and our bodies have not signed the treaty. Tens of millions of people now work through hours their biology never agreed to sell.

Meanwhile the one darkness we never could touch — the sky itself — has become, for most of humanity, a rumor. This is a strange kind of loss, because the dark sky is not empty. It is the deepest archive we have. Every star you see is a message years in transit; the light of Andromeda, the farthest thing your naked eye can perceive, is two and a half million years old — it left before our genus had quite settled into its modern shape. Looking up at night is the only form of time travel we possess: the sky is the past, directly observed. Whole cultures lived inside that archive. Aboriginal Australian astronomers read the heavens for tens of thousands of years, and one of their great constellations — the Emu in the Sky — is drawn not in stars but in darkness: a shadow-bird traced along the Coalsack, the dark nebula beside the Southern Cross. A constellation made of night. Sailors carried hand-held instruments called nocturnals for reading the hour off the wheeling stars — clocks made of darkness.

And I want to argue for the experience of the thing. Under a genuinely dark sky — and there are still such skies, on high deserts and remote islands and in the reserves that DarkSky International protects like nature preserves of nothing — the Milky Way is not a faint smudge. It is a structure. It has cliffs and channels; it rises like weather; in the right conditions it is bright enough to cast the faintest shadow. The great secret of true darkness is vertical. The city sky is a dome, low and close, a ceiling. The real sky is not a ceiling at all. Watch long enough and you can see it working: stars climbing out of the horizon, the whole field of them wheeling with the planet's turn, and then the vertigo arrives — you are not looking up, you are hanging off a moving sphere. Ancestors, scale, motion: no planetarium sells that feeling, because it cannot be faked. It requires the dark.

The reclamation has begun, and it is worth noticing what shape it takes. Towns dim their streetlights during migration season. Dark-sky reserves put formal borders around darkness and defend them like watershed. Astronomers lobby for shielding ordinances with the ardor of conservationists — which is what they are, conservationists of night. And individuals find small versions: the walk without the phone, the lamp left off after dinner, the deliberate blackout treated once a year as a holiday rather than a failure. We protect what we can still experience, which is the real argument for keeping some of the dark findable — not for the stars alone, but because the dark is where our own deep habits live: the two sleeps, the watch, the unlit hour in which the mind, left unsupervised for a while, remembers what it is.

Which is why I have come to think of a blackout, honestly, as a letter from an old friend. The grid fails and the century exits the room, and there — embarrassingly, unexpectedly — is the night of our species, holding its old position, waiting with a patience that ought to humble us. The dark was never the absence of something. It is the presence of everything else: the unlit majority of the universe, the rest-time, the deep; the place where the past arrives as starlight and the body's oldest rhythms keep their appointments. We didn't conquer the night. We have mostly just been keeping the curtains drawn. Every so often — and it takes so little: a switched-off lamp, an open door, a town that agrees to look up together — it is worth letting the oldest country back in.
